question: The utility replaces the transformer that feeds your plant. Under MTS Appendix C, which studies need updating?
choices: Only the incident-energy analysis
Only the one-line and the load-flow study
All five studies
Only the short-circuit study
explanation: A change in the utility or source is one of the rows in Appendix C that triggers every study. Available fault current changes, so everything downstream of it changes too. Source: ANSI/NETA MTS-2023 Appendix C.

question: Nothing in a facility has changed, but the last engineering update was five years ago. MTS Appendix C calls for updating:
choices: Every study, including coordination and load flow
Only the coordination study
One-line, short-circuit, and incident energy
None of them until something changes
explanation: Appendix C ties the five-year mark to the one-line, short-circuit, and incident-energy columns. It does not mark coordination or load flow for that row. Source: ANSI/NETA MTS-2023 Appendix C.

question: Which change does MTS Appendix C list as an example of a change in system impedance, configuration, or loading?
choices: Adding power-factor correction capacitors
Repainting the switchgear
Replacing a revenue meter with the same model
Relabeling panel schedules
explanation: Note 1 of Appendix C lists examples such as transformer kVA or impedance, conductor size or length, motor additions, high-efficiency motors, and power-factor capacitors. Each one changes fault current or flow. Source: ANSI/NETA MTS-2023 Appendix C note 1.

question: One project document lists the calculations, design decisions, and product selections the engineer used to meet the owner's goals and the governing codes. ECS calls this document the:
choices: Basis of Design (BOD)
Owner's Project Requirements (OPR)
Commissioning plan
Energization plan
explanation: The BOD explains how the design meets the OPR and the applicable codes and standards, in narrative and itemized form. The OPR states what the owner needs. The commissioning plan organizes the commissioning work itself. Source: ANSI/NETA ECS-2024 6.3 and Appendix A.

question: The owner's document says the data center must ride through a utility loss with no interruption to the critical load, lists budget limits, and defines how success will be measured. In ECS terms this is the:
choices: Basis of Design (BOD)
Short-circuit and coordination study
Final commissioning report
Owner's Project Requirements (OPR)
explanation: The OPR states the functional requirements and how the owner expects to use and operate the facility: goals, measurable performance criteria, cost considerations, benchmarks, and success criteria. The BOD is the designer's answer to it. Source: ANSI/NETA ECS-2024 6.2.

question: Under ECS-2024, who should develop the commissioning plan, and when?
choices: The electrical contractor, after all ATS acceptance tests pass
The commissioning authority, starting in design
The utility, at the time of service energization
The owner's maintenance staff, after turnover
explanation: ECS has the commissioning authority start the plan in the design phase. The commissioning team then updates and expands it through construction, acceptance, and occupancy. Everyone works from the latest version. Source: ANSI/NETA ECS-2024 6.4.2 and 6.4.3.

question: ECS divides the general commissioning tasks into pre-energization, energization, and post-energization. Which task belongs in post-energization?
choices: Verifying that temporary protective grounds have been removed
A thermographic survey under load per Section 9
Developing a written energization plan
Verifying CT circuits have a single point ground
explanation: The infrared survey needs load, so it comes after energization, along with post-energization fluid and gas analysis and load checks. Removing grounds is an energization step. The energization plan and CT checks are pre-energization tasks. Source: ANSI/NETA ECS-2024 7.1.A, 7.1.B, 7.1.C.

question: Under ECS-2024, which item is the owner's representative responsible for giving the commissioning organization?
choices: Timely notice of deficiencies found during commissioning
The final commissioning report
A calibration program for test instruments
Current IED setting files and relay logic diagrams
explanation: Section 4.1 puts the studies, setting sheets, IED setting files, logic diagrams, as-built plans, OPR, and BOD on the owner's side. Deficiency notices, the final report, and instrument calibration are the commissioning organization's job. Source: ANSI/NETA ECS-2024 4.1 and 4.2; 5.3.

question: The electrical contractor who installed a new substation offers to commission it with its own crew to save money. ECS-2024 says the commissioning organization should be:
choices: An independent third party
Any firm that holds the installation contract
The equipment manufacturer's field service group
The installing contractor, if a PE signs the report
explanation: ECS requires an unbiased, independent third-party commissioning organization that regularly does electrical commissioning. The installer can't objectively evaluate its own work. Source: ANSI/NETA ECS-2024 3.1.

question: Every component in a new lineup passed its ATS acceptance tests. Under ECS-2024, why isn't commissioning finished yet?
choices: ATS results expire after 30 days and must be repeated
ECS requires each ATS test to be repeated at a higher voltage
The system must still be proven against the OPR and BOD
Commissioning only begins after the first year of operation
explanation: ECS builds on ATS: individual components are validated by factory and field tests, then interconnections and the system are tested in part and in whole. Post-energization includes confirming the whole system behaves as the OPR, the BOD, and the approved sequence of operations call for. Source: ANSI/NETA ECS-2024 1.1.1, 6.1.3, 7.1.C.8.

question: Which item must the ECS-2024 commissioning report include?
choices: Only the issues that were resolved before turnover
The test technicians' certification exam scores
An issues log with open and closed items
A copy of every manufacturer's catalog
explanation: The report includes the final commissioning plan, test results, systems that don't meet the OPR, a resolution plan for incomplete tasks, as-left IED settings, progress reports, and an issues log with both open and closed items. Source: ANSI/NETA ECS-2024 5.4.

question: A new 69-13.8 kV substation has transformer differential protection. Beyond relay testing, ECS-2024 lists which medium-voltage tasks around the differential scheme?
choices: Through-fault primary injection, then operate and restraint checks
Only a visual check that the 87 relay is powered
A dc withstand of the CT secondaries, then a relay self-test at energization
Disabling the 87 during energization until load reaches 40%
explanation: For medium voltage, ECS adds verifying differential schemes per the OPR and primary-injection through-fault testing in pre-energization. During energization it has you verify correct operate and restraint quantities to the differential protection. Source: ANSI/NETA ECS-2024 7.2.A.33, 7.2.A.34, 7.2.B.7.

question: A new feeder lineup is being commissioned. Under ECS Section 9, the thermographic survey should be done at:
choices: Any load, since delta-T is independent of current
Normal circuit loading, with no minimum
No load, to get a clean baseline
Maximum possible load, at least 40% of nominal
explanation: ECS asks for maximum possible loading but no less than 40% of nominal, referring to NFPA 70B. ATS Section 9 says normal circuit loading. MTS says maximum possible loading with no stated floor. Source: ANSI/NETA ECS-2024 9.3.3; ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 Section 9; ANSI/NETA MTS-2023 Section 9.
reference: ANSI/NETA ECS-2024 9.3.3; ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 Section 9; ANSI/NETA MTS-2023 Section 9

question: At turnover under ECS-2024 Section 10, what happens to the commissioning organization's locks and tags?
choices: They stay on until the first maintenance outage
Removed and replaced by operator locks and tags
They are transferred to the owner without change
They are removed only after the warranty expires
explanation: Turnover is formal and documented. The operator is told about outstanding deficiencies and abnormal conditions, gets the documentation, and the commissioning locks and tags are replaced by the operator's where needed. Source: ANSI/NETA ECS-2024 10.

question: During energization of a new automatic transfer switch, ECS 8.3 has you do a load transfer test. What is checked besides the fact that the load moves?
choices: That the generator's PI is above 2.0
That the transfer time meets the project requirements
That the switch passes a 10-minute insulation-resistance test
That the normal source fails within 1 cycle
explanation: ECS asks you to transfer the actual connected load and monitor the transfer time against the specified project requirements. With several transfer switches or other protective devices, coordination tests verify the sequencing too. Source: ANSI/NETA ECS-2024 8.3.B.10 and B.11.

question: A PDU is fed from a UPS. The UPS has an input breaker, a battery breaker, a static-bypass input, and a maintenance bypass. A tech opens and locks only the UPS input breaker and calls the PDU dead. What did he miss?
choices: The battery and bypass paths are also sources
Nothing, since the UPS input is the only utility connection
Only the battery breaker; the bypass paths are interlocked
Only the downstream PDU main; the UPS is upstream
explanation: Establishing an electrically safe work condition starts with finding every possible source from current drawings, then opening a disconnect for each. A UPS has several: the inverter on battery, the static bypass, and the maintenance bypass. Source: NFPA 70E-2024 120.6(1) and 120.6(2).

question: What makes breaker-failure relaying (50BF) different from remote backup protection?
choices: It replaces the primary relay on the feeder
It only operates when the dc battery has failed
It closes the failed breaker again after a short time delay
It catches a stuck breaker locally, not remotely
explanation: IEEE 242 calls breaker-failure relaying local breaker backup. Remote backup relies on relays at other terminals and is slower and less selective. When testing 50BF, ATS 7.9.1 covers current-supervision pickup, time delays, and the initiate inputs and trip outputs. Source: IEEE 242-2001, 14.5.7; ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.9.1.

question: Before connecting a test set to an in-service relay, in what order does Werstiuk recommend isolating and restoring circuits?
choices: Isolate ac first, then trip; on restore, put trip back first
Trip circuit out first; on restore, ac back first, then trip
Leave the trip circuit in so you can see a real breaker operation
Isolate only the ac circuits; the trip circuit doesn't matter
explanation: Disabling the trip path first keeps a nuisance trip from happening as ac circuits are disturbed. On restore, ac goes back first so you can confirm no trip signals are present before the trip and close circuits are put back. Source: Werstiuk, The Relay Testing Handbook: Principles and Practice, ch. 18, 1.
reference: Werstiuk, The Relay Testing Handbook: Principles and Practice, ch. 18, 1

question: A tech wants to time a relay by putting the test set's timer input across the relay's trip contact while the trip circuit is still connected. Werstiuk's warning is that:
choices: The timer will read the ac ripple and give false times
A low-impedance timer input can trip the breaker
The relay will lock out its own targets
The dc will damage the relay's output contact
explanation: Some test-set sensing inputs act almost like a jumper. Across a live trip contact they can energize the trip coil. Isolate the trip circuit or use a connection that can't complete it. Source: Werstiuk, The Relay Testing Handbook: Principles and Practice, ch. 18, Figure 18-4.
reference: Werstiuk, The Relay Testing Handbook: Principles and Practice, ch. 18, Figure 18-4

question: In a short-circuit study, which calculated current is used to check the interrupting duty of low-voltage breakers and fuses?
choices: The 30-cycle time-delayed current
The interrupting-network current used for MV breakers
The steady-state load-flow current
The first-cycle (half-cycle) current
explanation: IEEE 399 explains that the first-cycle network gives the momentary (close-and-latch) duty for MV and HV gear, while for LV gear that same result is the duty the device must interrupt. The interrupting-network results are used for MV and HV breakers. Source: IEEE 399-1997, 7.4.1 and Table 7-2 notes.

question: Time-delayed short-circuit currents (beyond 6 cycles, up to 30) are used to check time-overcurrent relay sensitivity. How does IEEE 399 model motors for that case?
choices: Motor contributions are left out
Motors are modeled with subtransient reactance
Motor contribution is doubled for safety
Only induction motors above 50 hp are included
explanation: By then motor contributions have decayed, so they are left out, and generators use transient or higher reactance. These currents also carry no dc offset. Source: IEEE 399-1997, 7.4.1.

question: A plant changes relay settings on its main breakers but changes no equipment. Under MTS Appendix C, which study is not marked for update?
choices: The coordination study
The incident-energy analysis
The short-circuit study
The one-line diagram
explanation: A change in protective devices or settings marks the one-line, coordination, incident energy, and load flow. Fault current doesn't change when only settings change, so the short-circuit study isn't marked. Source: ANSI/NETA MTS-2023 Appendix C.

question: A plant adds several large motors to an existing bus. Under MTS Appendix C (change in impedance, configuration, or loading), which updates are marked?
choices: All five studies
Only coordination and load flow, nothing else at all
One-line, short-circuit, and incident energy
Incident energy only
explanation: That row marks the one-line, short-circuit, and incident-energy columns. Motor additions are one of the note 1 examples because motors contribute fault current. Source: ANSI/NETA MTS-2023 Appendix C and note 1.
reference: ANSI/NETA MTS-2023 Appendix C and note 1

question: MTS Appendix B base interval for full electrical testing of a liquid-filled transformer is 24 months. The unit is in poor condition and serves a high-reliability load. The adjusted interval is:
choices: 6 months
12 months
24 months
60 months
explanation: The Appendix B matrix factor for high reliability and poor condition is 0.25. 24 x 0.25 = 6 months. Source: ANSI/NETA MTS-2023 Appendix B.

question: A medium-voltage breaker has a 36-month base interval for full electrical testing. It is in good condition on a low-reliability-requirement circuit. Using MTS Appendix B, the interval becomes:
choices: 18 months
36 months
54 months
90 months
explanation: Low reliability with good condition has a factor of 2.5. 36 x 2.5 = 90 months. Source: ANSI/NETA MTS-2023 Appendix B.

question: A microprocessor relay has a 36-month base interval for electrical testing. It is in average condition and protects a high-reliability process. Using MTS Appendix B, test it every:
choices: 9 months
18 months
36 months
72 months
explanation: High reliability with average condition has a factor of 0.50. 36 x 0.5 = 18 months. Source: ANSI/NETA MTS-2023 Appendix B.

question: On industrial machinery, the protective bonding circuit is checked with an impedance instrument. What is the NFPA 79 maximum?
choices: 1 ohm
0.1 ohm, allowing for the test lead impedance
25 ohms
0.5 megohm
explanation: With the impedance-meter method, the effective ground-fault current path must measure 0.1 ohm or less once the test circuit's own impedance is taken out. Source: NFPA 79-2024, 18.2(1).

question: Using the NFPA 79 10 A method on a 14 AWG protective conductor, what is the largest voltage drop allowed?
explanation: The alternative continuity method drives at least 10 A at 50 or 60 Hz from a SELV source and measures the drop. Table 18.2 sets the limit by wire size, and for 14 AWG it is 1.9 V. Thinner wire is allowed more. Source: NFPA 79-2024, 18.2(2) and Table 18.2.

question: When NFPA 79 insulation resistance testing applies, what test voltage and minimum value are used?
choices: 500 V dc, at least 1 megohm between power conductors and the protective bonding circuit
1000 V dc, at least 100 megohms
250 V dc, at least 0.5 megohm
2500 V dc, at least 25 megohms
explanation: Apply 500 V dc between the power circuit conductors and the ground-fault path. The reading must be at least 1 megohm. Sections of a large machine may be tested one at a time. Source: NFPA 79-2024, 18.3.

question: An NFPA 79 voltage test is applied to a machine's primary circuits. Which setup matches the standard?
choices: Apply 2121 V ac for 1 minute
Apply 1000 V dc instantly for 10 minutes
Raise gradually to 1500 V ac, or its 2121 V dc peak equivalent, and hold at least 1 s, from a supply of at least 500 VA
Apply 500 V ac for 1 s from any source
explanation: Bring the voltage up from zero to 1500 V ac, or the 2121 V dc equivalent, from the primary conductors to the ground-fault path, and hold at least one second without breakdown. 1500 × √2 ≈ 2121, which is why those numbers pair. Disconnect parts that can't take the voltage. Source: NFPA 79-2024, 18.4.

question: A machine's wiring was modified in the field. Which NFPA 79 verification is always required, and what about the rest?
choices: All five tests are mandatory on every machine every time
Only the voltage test is required
Ground-fault path continuity is always verified and documented; the other tests are done where they apply, and changed parts are retested
Nothing, if the machine was listed
explanation: The ground-fault return path is always proved continuous and written up. Insulation, voltage, residual-voltage and function tests happen when judged necessary. After a change, the affected portion is re-verified. Source: NFPA 79-2024, 18.1 and 18.7.

question: A stationary fuel cell room has combustible gas detection. Under NFPA 853, at what levels does it alarm and shut off the fuel?
choices: Alarm at 25% of the LFL; shut off fuel at 60% of the LFL
Alarm at 10% LFL; shut off at 25% LFL
Alarm at 50% LFL; shut off at 100% LFL
Alarm only; no fuel shutoff
explanation: The detector alarms at a quarter of the lowest lower flammable limit for the gas and closes the fuel supply at 60%. Put the detectors where leaks are likely for the fuel used. Source: NFPA 853-2025, 8.1.5.4 to 8.1.5.7.

question: At a generating plant, two outdoor oil-filled transformers sit near each other. Under NFPA 850, how is the separation decided?
choices: No separation is ever needed outdoors
Only by the transformer maker's catalog
By NFPA 70B maintenance intervals
By the documented fire protection design basis, with fire barriers, distance or another approved method (Table 6.1.4.3)
explanation: Outdoor oil-insulated transformers are kept apart from each other and from buildings by fire barriers, distance or another approved method. The analysis is recorded in the fire protection design basis document, and the table gives the 2-hour firewall or spacing options. Source: NFPA 850-2026, 6.1.4.1 to 6.1.4.3 and Table 6.1.4.3.
